text: dsh-journal-calendar 是一款面向 DSH 网页客户端的每日记事与日历插件。它在 Host 侧注册 journal_record 工具和 journal 远程服务，并在右侧栏提供日历卡片。用户可以记录已发生的记忆或计划中的待办，按日期查看每日条目，标记待办完成，并编辑提示词中的记事职责句。条目按天保存为本机 JSON 文件，记忆可链接回记录它的会话。适合希望持续整理每日进展和计划、并从网页侧栏回顾的 DSH 用户；无需 API 密钥或外部服务。

dsh-journal-calendar adds daily journaling to DSH with a journal_record tool and web sidebar calendar. Record plans and memories, browse by day, mark todos complete, edit the journaling prompt, and return to the source conversation. Entries are local files; no API key is needed.
想让 DSH 把每天做过的事和计划记下来。
有没有能在网页侧栏按日期翻看日记和待办的日历？
我希望把待办和已完成事项分开记录，还能勾选完成。
能不能从日记里的记忆直接回到当时的会话？
I want my assistant to keep a daily log of plans and things accomplished.
想把当天的计划和重要进展保存成可回看的日记。
Can a journal entry link back to the conversation where it was created?
Can I browse journal entries by day in a web calendar sidebar?
dsh-journal-calendar 的功能「每日记录」：用 journal_record 保存 todo 或 memory 条目，可填写标题、详情、标签和日期；相同 id 重试不会重复写入。
dsh-journal-calendar 的功能「日历浏览」：网页右侧栏显示月份网格和每日条目，按天呈现待办与记忆，并用标记概览各日记录。
dsh-journal-calendar 的功能「完成待办」：在选中日期的日历卡片中切换待办完成状态，状态写回日记文件并更新日历展示。
dsh-journal-calendar 的功能「编辑记事职责」：日历标题旁的编辑入口可修改提示词中的记事职责句；保存后写入 duty.md，下一次提示词组装时读取。

dsh-journal-calendar README · dsh-journal-calendar：English | [中文](README.zh.md)

A daily journal and calendar for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (DSH). The agent records what you did and what you intend to do into one JSON file per day, and the Web UI draws those files as a calendar in the right sidebar.

dsh-journal-calendar README · What it contributes：One bundle row mounts all three faces:

| Face | What it is |
|---|---|
| Host service | `journal`, a Remote namespace over `$DSH_HOME/journal` |
| Tool | `journal_record`, plus a standing-duty prompt section |
| Browser half | the calendar card, a right-sidebar tab |

The card shows a month grid with a marker per day, and below it the selected day's `TO DO` and `MEMORY` sections. Todos carry a checkbox that writes straight back to the day file.

dsh-journal-calendar README · Install：```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-journal-calendar
```

Then reload the page. The **日历 / Journal** tab appears in the right sidebar.

dsh-journal-calendar README · Install：That resolves the published package from your configured npm registry and ships a prebuilt tarball, so nothing is compiled on your machine and no build authorization is needed. `dsh plugin` forwards to pnpm, so pnpm must be on the machine. Pin a version with `dsh-journal-calendar@0.3.0`. A bare name resolves to the newest release pnpm's supply-chain policy already trusts: that policy holds back any version published less than 24 hours ago, so pin the exact version to install the latest one right after a release. To remove it again:

dsh-journal-calendar README · Install：```sh
dsh plugin --profile web remove dsh-journal-calendar
```

dsh-journal-calendar README · Installing the release tarball instead：Every release attaches that same prebuilt tarball to its GitHub release, which covers a registry that has not mirrored the release yet:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add https://github.com/crease123/dsh-journal-calendar/releases/download/v0.3.0/dsh-journal-calendar-0.3.0.tgz
```

dsh-journal-calendar README · Installing from the repository instead：Building from source works too, and is what you get before a release exists:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add git+https://github.com/crease123/dsh-journal-calendar
```

dsh-journal-calendar README · Installing from the repository instead：That fetches **source**, so it builds on your machine. The first attempt stops, because pnpm refuses to run a git-hosted package's build script until you allow that exact package. `dsh` prints the key to paste under `allowBuilds` in the profile's `pnpm-workspace.yaml`; add it and re-run. Treat that authorization as permission for this package's code to run on your machine at install time, and pin a commit (`…#<sha>`) if you want the installed code to stay fixed.

dsh-journal-calendar README · Installing from the repository instead：Every path ends at the same prebuilt artifact: the release tarball is byte-identical to the package the registry serves (one sha1 covers both), and both install with no authorization step at all; the `git+https://` install builds on your machine through its authorization step. Each boots with no warnings and reads and writes real day files.

dsh-journal-calendar README · Where your entries live：One JSON file per day, at `$DSH_HOME/journal/<YYYY-MM-DD>.json` (`~/.dsh/journal` by default). Each file is the complete record of that day:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "date": "2026-09-30",
  "entries": [

Point it somewhere else by giving the row a `dir`:

```yaml
- id: journal
  name: dsh-journal-calendar
  config:
    dir: /absolute/path/to/journal

dsh-journal-calendar README · Where your entries live：**Your entries are plain files you own.** Anything that can read JSON can read them, and editing them by hand is supported: keep every entry `id` and the top-level `"version": 1`.

The service treats a file it cannot parse as a hard error rather than rebuilding it, because silently rewriting a day would destroy the record it holds.

dsh-journal-calendar README · What the agent does with it：The plugin registers the `journal_record` tool and one prompt sentence telling the agent that recording is part of its job. The tool takes a `kind` (`todo` = an intention, checkable; `memory` = something that happened), a one-line `title`, and optionally `detail`, `tags`, `date`, and `time`.

Recording the same `id` twice returns the stored entry instead of appending a second one, so a retried tool call is safe.
section: What the agent does with it

text: dsh-journal-calendar README · Jumping back to the conversation：An entry recorded from a conversation also stores that Session and the turn it came from, so a memory in the card is a link: clicking one switches to the conversation and scrolls to the turn the entry was recorded in, with a brief highlight. Entries written outside a conversation (hand-edited files, or anything recorded before this existed) carry no source and stay plain text. The scroll addresses turns through the Web client's `data-chat-turn` attribute; if a future client stops publishing it, the click still opens the conversation and simply does not scroll.

dsh-journal-calendar README · Editing the duty sentence：That prompt sentence is yours to rewrite. The calendar card carries a ✎ button beside the month heading: it opens an inline editor prefilled with the text now in effect, with Save, Reset, and Cancel. The text lands in `$DSH_HOME/journal/duty.md` (beside the day files, following `dir`), and the **next message** already carries it — the section is re-read on every prompt assembly, with no reload. Clearing the editor and saving removes the file and restores the built-in sentence. The limit is 2000 characters; the text is inserted verbatim, so `{{` in it is your own writing, not a variable reference.

dsh-journal-calendar README · Development：```sh
pnpm install
pnpm run build      # tsc (both faces) then tsdown (both bundles)
pnpm run test
pnpm run typecheck

The repository owns its own tool roots — `pnpm-workspace.yaml` and `vitest.config.ts` exist so pnpm and Vitest do not walk up into an ancestor repository when this package is developed inside a DSH checkout.

dsh-journal-calendar README · The generated Remote artifacts：`generated/` holds the Typert artifacts (`typert.host.*`, `typert.remote-client.*`) that the Host contributes and the browser bundle inlines. They are **generated, not built here**:

dsh-journal-calendar README · The generated Remote artifacts：`@deepseek-ai/dsh-typert-generator` discovers contributing packages only under `<root>/packages`, and identifies `TypertRemoteService` by requiring that symbol to be declared in a *registered* package. A package that takes `@deepseek-ai/dsh-typert-protocol` from `node_modules` therefore can never be analyzed in place.

dsh-journal-calendar README · The generated Remote artifacts：`pnpm run regen-typert` bridges that gap by itself: it copies this repository's `src/` into the checkout under the upstream experimental name, registers the scaffold in the Host aggregate for the length of one run, runs the generator, and restores the checkout byte-for-byte afterwards. Only `packages/typert/generator` must be built in the checkout (`pnpm run build`); the script refuses to emit an artifact that does not name every Remote method this package declares, so a stale copy cannot pass silently:

dsh-journal-calendar README · The generated Remote artifacts：```sh
DSH_CHECKOUT=/path/to/deepseek-harness pnpm run regen-typert
```

The checkout's `packages/typert/generator` must be built first. Rerun whenever a `@Remote` method's name, signature, or return type changes, or when the Remote error table changes. `scripts/typert-identity.mjs` states the identity rewrite the artifacts need, and `tests/build-artifacts.spec.ts` fails the suite if a regenerated artifact still names the upstream package — the Typert loader rejects such a contribution at boot.

dsh-journal-calendar README · The generated Remote artifacts：**Restart the DSH host after regenerating.** The Typert loader registers a package's Host face from its `./typert` export and caches the imported manifest per package name for the life of the process, while a hot reload of the package withdraws its strict definitions without committing a replacement. The running card then fails every call with `its strict definition was withdrawn and SRC fallback is forbidden`, even though the artifacts on disk are correct. A restart registers them once, from the new files.
dsh-journal-calendar README · The publint warning about `./client`：`npx publint` reports one warning: `./lib/client.js` is CommonJS inside a `"type": "module"` package, so Node would read it as ESM.

dsh-journal-calendar README · The publint warning about `./client`：Leave it. The browser module table fetches that file's bytes and materializes it through `window.__ModuleLoader__.load({ id, factory })`; Node never resolves or imports it, so the extension it is judged by never applies. Renaming it to `.cjs` to silence the warning would depart from every DSH client plugin, all of which ship `lib/client.js` under `"type": "module"`.

dsh-journal-calendar README · Compatibility：Declared through `peerDependencies` and `engines.dsh`. Verified end to end against DSH `0.1.7-rc.1` and `0.2.0-rc.2`: install, boot, bundle delivery, and the `month` / `day` / `setDone` endpoints reading and writing real day files.

On Node `22.19.0` and `26.4.0`, the same acceptance run passes and the host artifacts load. Node `24` and `25` sit between two verified versions; `engines.node` names the two release lines DSH itself supports.

dsh-journal-calendar README · Compatibility：Every DSH range names each supported release line explicitly, for example `>=0.1.7-rc.1 <0.2.0 || >=0.2.0-rc.1 <0.3.0-0`. This is not decoration: node-semver only lets a prerelease version satisfy a range when a comparator in that range shares the version's exact `major.minor.patch` tuple *and* carries a prerelease tag itself. A broad-looking `>=0.1.7-rc.1 <0.3.0` silently excludes `0.2.0-rc.2` — pnpm only warns, and the install resolves to something neither side intended. `tests/manifest.spec.ts` pins the ranges to the versions an acceptance run exercised.

dsh-journal-calendar README · Compatibility：DSH reads these ranges at install time and refuses an incompatible plugin, restoring the profile manifest — verified by installing a deliberately-incompatible copy and watching it rejected. But DSH evaluates them with `includePrerelease`, so a range too broad for your package manager still passes there. That asymmetry is exactly why the ranges are pinned by a test instead of eyeballed.

dsh-journal-calendar README · Publishing：The repository is the source of truth for the npm package and for the community listing.

```sh
npm login --registry https://registry.npmjs.org
npm publish
```

dsh-journal-calendar README · Publishing：`prepack` builds before the tarball is written, so `npm publish` ships compiled output and installs need no build step. `publishConfig` pins both the public access level and the official registry, because a machine configured against a mirror would otherwise publish somewhere no one else can install from. Check what would ship with `npm publish --dry-run`.

dsh-journal-calendar README · Publishing：npm requires two-factor authentication for publishing. An account without 2FA — or a token without **Bypass 2FA** — cannot publish directly: the upload lands in the staging area instead (`npm stage publish`), and the version goes live only through `npm stage approve <stage-id>`, which proves presence in the browser. Enabling 2FA on the account is what makes that approval complete; without it, the approval cannot prove anything and the registry rejects it.

dsh-journal-calendar README · Publishing：To list it in the [dsh-market](https://github.com/dsh-market/dsh-market) plugin market, open a PR that adds **one file** — `data/plugins/crease123__dsh-journal-calendar.yml` — to the [awesome-dsh-plugin](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin) registry:

dsh-journal-calendar README · Publishing：```yaml
url: https://github.com/crease123/dsh-journal-calendar
name: crease123/dsh-journal-calendar
category: memory
tarball: https://github.com/crease123/dsh-journal-calendar/releases/download/v0.3.0/dsh-journal-calendar-0.3.0.tgz

dsh-journal-calendar README · Publishing：The description is long on purpose: the registry already lists `AloneFu/dsh-calendar-plugin`, which also draws a month grid with per-day markers in the sidebar. The difference is what the entries are and who writes them — that plugin views an existing Obsidian vault, while this one has the agent maintain its own day files under the DSH home. A registry reviewer checks an entry against the plugin, and asks whether an existing entry already covers it, so the line has to carry that distinction.

dsh-journal-calendar README · Publishing：The registry's `url` must match the repository exactly, and the repository must carry the `dsh-plugin` GitHub topic and be at least one day old. The published package's `repository` field points at the same URL, which is what links the two.

dsh-journal-calendar README · Known limitations：- **The Web UI is required to see the calendar.** On a headless profile the tool still records entries; nothing draws them.
- **Regenerating the Remote artifacts needs a DSH checkout.** Changing a `@Remote` method's signature is not a self-contained operation here.
- **Days are grouped by the local date of the machine running DSH.** A day file does not carry a timezone, so a laptop that changes timezone mid-travel can attribute an entry to the neighbouring day.
- **Jumping back to a conversation relies on the Web client.** The card locates the turn through the `data-chat-turn` attribute; a client that stops publishing it opens the conversation without scrolling, and entries written before the anchor existed have no source at all.
- **`todo` here is not `todo_write`.** The calendar's todos are durable, one JSON file per day; the built-in `todo_write` tool is a per-session list. Both read as "记录一下" to a model, and no prompt currently distinguishes them.
